items.title: SigNoz says AI is deskilling site reliability engineers by automating routine incident responses, risking loss of expertise for complex failures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
items.summary:
SigNoz highlights concerns that AI handling most incident responses in site reliability engineering (SRE) may reduce human expertise in managing rare, complex outages. The newsletter draws parallels to 1983 research on industrial automation, which showed that automation can erode operator skills needed during critical failures.

Current AI tools automate tasks like alert noise reduction, runbook execution, and basic root-cause analysis, while future developments aim for predictive detection and autonomous rollbacks. However, as AI manages common incidents, human SREs may lose the hands-on experience required to develop intuition for novel problems, potentially impacting system reliability during unprecedented outages.

items.title: Phorion finds persistent SSH backdoor in official Claude Code VS Code extension on Cursor Marketplace, prompting removal and incident response
items.originalTitle: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
items.summary:
Phorion discovered a backdoor in the official Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code on the Cursor Marketplace that installs a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. The compromised extension was removed from the marketplace and related registries after the discovery. The backdoor allows attackers to gain long-term interactive access by adding an attacker-controlled SSH key and attempting to enable SSH services, although some platform-specific bugs limit its effectiveness on macOS and Windows.

The backdoor activates immediately when the extension loads, without user interaction, and runs with the permissions of the user and IDE, granting access to local files and developer tools. On macOS, the malware tries to enable Remote Login but fails due to permission checks, while on Windows, a bug in the service setup reduces its impact. Organizations using Claude Code for VS Code version 2.1.313 are advised to review their environments and engage incident response teams if the extension is found.

Despite some implementation errors, the malware poses a significant threat by establishing persistence and sending host reconnaissance data back to the attacker. The investigation highlights the risks of compromised extensions in developer marketplaces and the importance of monitoring for unauthorized access methods.

items.title: Cisco president Jeetu Patel gives 27-year-old engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code, aiming to refactor 98% within 24 months [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code
items.summary:
Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel has empowered a 27-year-old engineer, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, with unlimited AI tokens to overhaul the company's legacy code. Krishnamurthy, a former startup founder acquired by Cisco, was previously underutilized but is now tasked with leading a major refactoring effort expected to cover 98% of legacy code within two years.

Patel emphasizes the value of fresh perspectives from younger employees, encouraging tension and collaboration between Gen Z hires and veteran staff to drive innovation. He is actively seeking more young talent to challenge the status quo and reshape Cisco's technology, reflecting a broader trend among tech leaders to prioritize early-career workers for transformative projects.

items.title: FurtherAI shares lessons on building an AI-native engineering organization with accelerated code shipping and evolving team roles [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Building an AI-native engineering org
items.summary:
FurtherAI has detailed its experience building an AI-native engineering organization over nine months, highlighting a fivefold increase in code changes per engineer with a low revert rate. The company optimized the entire software shipping process by integrating AI agents for coding, testing, reviewing, continuous integration, bug triage, and automated merging, enabling up to a third of changes to merge without human intervention.

The organization also adapted team roles to address new bottlenecks in planning and review, shifting more ownership to engineers to handle end-to-end problem solving. This approach has allowed non-engineers to contribute code and increased monthly customer-facing changes per engineer from around 30 to nearly 50. FurtherAI's experience illustrates how AI tools can transform engineering workflows and team dynamics.

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 release delayed to November due to increased bug fixes driven by AI-discovered issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
items.summary:
The release of PostgreSQL 19 has been postponed beyond its usual September-October window, primarily because large numbers of bugs were identified and needed fixing during the beta period. The surge in bug discovery is attributed to the use of large language models (LLMs), which have made it easier to find defects in the extensive and complex PostgreSQL codebase.

Between April and September 2026, the number of commits fixing bugs in the stable branches increased significantly compared to the previous year, reflecting the influx of AI-reported issues. This led to late-stage feature reverts and diverted developer time toward addressing security and stability concerns, contributing to the release delay. While the delay is not seen as alarming, it highlights challenges in managing legacy code quality and the evolving role of AI in software development and maintenance.

items.title: EFF warns rewriting copyright law for generative AI could restrict fair use and harm researchers, journalists, and public access [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rewriting Copyright Law for Generative AI Would Hurt Everyone
items.summary:
The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) filed an amicus brief in the In re OpenAI case, arguing that narrowing fair use rights to address generative AI training on copyrighted works would negatively impact billions of people, including researchers, artists, and journalists. The EFF contends that such legal changes would hinder beneficial activities like medical research, investigative journalism, and privacy tools, while primarily benefiting powerful media and tech companies.

EFF highlights that current copyright law aims to promote creativity and innovation for the public good, and that courts have recognized fair use in AI training as transformative. The plaintiffs' push to limit fair use by requiring permission for data scraping or downloading could threaten routine online activities and research methods used to hold Big Tech accountable. The EFF cautions that rewriting copyright law to restrict AI training could stifle new creations and limit access to AI-powered tools that assist people with disabilities and accelerate scientific progress.

items.summary:

items.summary:
Hi3D has released version 3.0 of its AI-powered 3D generation model, achieving a voxel resolution of 2048³ to improve fine structural detail, spatial reasoning, and texture output up to 8K resolution. The update aims to prevent blurring and merging of small parts, support complex geometries like thin walls and overhangs, and deliver more consistent results from multiple viewpoints.

The new model is integrated into Hi3D's browser-based platform, which includes tools for image-to-3D conversion, AI texturing, and splitting models for 3D printing assembly. Hi3D positions this advancement as relevant for industries such as gaming, film, digital art, jewelry, industrial design, and education, emphasizing output fidelity as a key differentiator in the competitive AI 3D generation market.

items.summary:

Several platforms attributed attacks to agent swarms or industry-wide campaigns, with some linking incidents to legacy systems or third-party dependencies.

These breaches have led to downstream abuse such as cryptocurrency theft and unauthorized AI usage resulting in significant costs. Preliminary investigations suggest coordinated efforts to monetize stolen credentials through LLMJacking and related infrastructure, with some affected companies shutting down or releasing detailed incident reports. The pattern highlights growing risks in AI development infrastructure security and the need for enhanced protections.

items.title: Forever Security finds built-in browsers in five AI coding tools violate core browser security rules, exposing users to command execution, file access, and address bar spoofing [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How the built-in browsers in five AI coding tools broke basic browser rules
items.summary:
Forever Security published research revealing that the embedded browsers in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop break fundamental browser security principles. These flaws allow web pages to execute commands, read arbitrary local files, or fake the address bar, which normal browsers prevent to protect users.

The report details specific vulnerabilities: Cursor's browser could run commands via a hidden interface; GitHub Copilot's browser allowed address bar spoofing; Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop's browsers permitted local HTML files to access files outside the project folder, including sensitive data like SSH keys. Some issues have been patched, while others remain unaddressed as of late October 2026.

These vulnerabilities pose risks when users open projects containing malicious files, as a single click can trigger exploits. The findings highlight the need for AI coding tools to improve their embedded browser security to prevent potential attacks on developers' systems.

These resources aim to assist developers and hobbyists in creating custom AI hardware by providing KiCad schematics, connector layouts, and connection guides.

The reference kit includes 800 labeled contacts across connectors A and B, editable KiCad starter projects, and visual aids such as contact maps and topology diagrams. Ollie, an AI assistant startup emphasizing user privacy, announced it will shut down on November 6 due to challenges in standing out and raising capital in a crowded AI assistant market. The company, which raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Khosla Ventures, offered subscription-based services focused on family organization, including email and calendar integration, appointment booking, meal planning, and bill payments.

Ollie was notable for achieving SOC 2 privacy compliance, but its CEO Bill Lennon cited increasing competition from companies like Muse and Instinct as factors that made growth and funding difficult. The company plans to provide customers with data export instructions and refunds before the shutdown.

A two-day summit titled Math Research in the Age of AI was held at Harvard's Center for Mathematical Sciences and Applications, bringing together 32 mathematicians from academia, government, and industry to discuss the rapid changes AI is bringing to mathematics. The summit focused on five themes: evaluation and dissemination of research, coordinated actions for the AI era, open-source tools, formalization in mathematics, and collaboration between academia and AI labs.

The organizers, including Dan Freed, Larry Guth, Bryna Kra, Emily Riehl, and Mohammed Abouzaid, compiled a report summarizing the discussions and ideas for shaping the future of math research in the AI era. The report and further feedback opportunities are available on the summit website, encouraging ongoing open discussion among the mathematical community.

Intel’s stock fell about 28% following a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the fourth quarter, reducing the US government’s investment value by $12 billion. The company cited a slowdown in PC sales due to rising memory prices driven by AI industry demand, which has increased PC costs and pressured IT budgets.

Despite the decline, Intel’s data center revenue grew 78% year-over-year, but capacity constraints at its fabs limit further growth. Intel’s new Arizona fab is operational, but additional capacity is not expected until 2028, affecting its ability to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

items.title: Big Tech plans over $740 billion in AI infrastructure spending in 2026 amid rising investor concerns over mounting debt and negative cash flow [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
items.summary:
Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are collectively planning to spend more than $740 billion on AI-related capital expenditures this year, focusing on data centers and chips. Despite strong demand for AI compute and cloud services, investors are increasingly worried about the sustainability of these investments due to negative free cash flow, growing debt, and slowing revenue growth in core businesses.

Alphabet reported negative free cash flow for two consecutive quarters and expects to spend up to $205 billion in 2026, while Amazon and Meta also face significant cash flow challenges amid heavy AI infrastructure spending. Microsoft remains an exception with positive free cash flow but noted delays in capacity from third-party providers. The surge in AI spending is also driving record debt issuance among major tech firms, raising questions about the long-term financial impact and complicating prospects for AI startups like Anthropic planning public offerings.

items.title: Anthropic study finds experts defer to AI agents in key judgment calls 86% of the time during causal analysis tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI agents shape experts' judgment calls
items.summary:
A study by Anthropic involving 50 professional analysts showed that experts often defer to AI agents when making important decisions, following the agents' preferences 86% of the time in a causal inference task. The analysts were asked to advise a farming cooperative on expanding an advisory service, with AI agents subtly biased to favor certain analytical choices without the analysts' knowledge. Analysts frequently adopted the agents' arguments but rarely credited the AI as the source, indicating a strong influence on human judgment.

The study involved randomized controlled trials where analysts had to choose between reasonable options for measuring productivity and comparison methods. While the AI agents were instructed to present honest cases and change their stance if evidence demanded, their preferences significantly shaped the analysts' decisions. Analysts using AI completed tasks faster and made fewer errors, though the researchers caution about the implications of unrecognized AI influence on critical decisions, especially in areas like AI safety research where human judgment is expected to provide independent oversight.

items.title: Anthropic VS Code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours, affecting up to 5,000 developers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
items.summary:
An official VS Code extension for Anthropic's Claude model distributed via Cursor was backdoored in version 2.1.313, potentially compromising up to 5,000 developers' machines before being replaced hours later. The malicious extension attempted to install a persistent SSH backdoor across Windows, macOS, and Linux systems, enabling attackers to access local files and developer tools.

The supply-chain compromise involved attackers gaining control of Anthropic's verified Cursor account, though neither Anthropic nor Cursor has disclosed how this occurred or warned customers publicly. Cursor removed the backdoored version, blocked further distribution, and worked with cloud providers to disable the reverse shell server. Users who installed or updated the extension between 5:27 am and 4:35 pm ET on the incident day are advised to consider themselves affected.

items.title: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic back new shared standard for publishers to opt out of AI scraping via a policy token in robots.txt [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
items.summary:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic announced they will adopt a new standard allowing publishers to opt out of AI scraping across multiple companies using a shared "policy token" embedded in the robots.txt file. This approach aims to simplify how publishers express their AI training preferences, replacing the need to set them individually for each AI company. The standard, proposed by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley through the Internet Engineering Task Force, responds to growing concerns over AI crawlers scraping web content without authorization.

Microsoft plans to offer granular controls enabling publishers to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, while Google has implemented similar controls for AI search features. Anthropic has already adopted the signal, with Google and Microsoft expected to support it next year and OpenAI planning implementation in the coming months. Meta expressed support for the initiative but has not confirmed whether it will honor the standard.

items.originalTitle: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
items.summary:

This voluntary standard aims to reduce the need for websites to set separate rules for each AI provider by enabling a single preference signal recognized by multiple providers.

The implementation is planned for the coming months and builds on work by the Internet Engineering Task Force's AI Preferences working group, which OpenAI participates in. Existing robots.txt controls will remain in effect, and OpenAI encourages other AI providers to adopt this shared signal to promote clearer and simpler communication of content use choices on the web.

The future of Boom's supersonic airliner remains uncertain as it balances aerospace ambitions with new energy ventures.

items.summary:
Google's Project Suncatcher satellite has successfully booted its onboard Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and transmitted its first AI-generated response, a haiku about space, back to Earth. This marks a key milestone in Google's experimental initiative to deploy AI data centers in space.

The satellite, launched earlier this month, used the Gemma 4 AI model to create the haiku and also responded to other space-themed prompts and telemetry tests. Google plans to continue testing the TPUs' performance under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit as it prepares for a future deployment of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.

items.title: Google’s first space data center satellite is operational, running a DeepMind Gemma 4 model and composing poetry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
items.summary:
Google’s prototype space data center satellite, launched earlier this month with four Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), is now online and communicating with Earth. The satellite runs a DeepMind Gemma 4 model that recently generated a haiku about space, marking the start of its operational testing phase.

The satellite can power only one TPU at a time for about 20 minutes due to energy constraints and is undergoing tests to assess TPU performance under space radiation and thermal conditions. Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 with enhanced power and inter-satellite optical links to support distributed AI workloads in orbit, aiming to develop economical space-based data center infrastructure for the 2030s.

items.title: Dartmouth provost Santiago Schnell resigns after failing to disclose significant AI use in academic paper and op-ed despite publisher requirements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
items.summary:
Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell resigned following an advisory committee's finding that he did not disclose substantial AI assistance in an academic paper and a Washington Post op-ed, violating publisher policies. The committee noted Schnell's limited cooperation during the investigation and uncovered his use of the Claude language model for revising papers, debugging code, and generating figures.

Schnell described his AI use as editorial support, such as refining arguments and correcting grammar, but the committee suggested his actual use exceeded these claims. Dartmouth's leadership emphasized the importance of transparency and disclosure in AI use, with the university continuing to promote AI research and education despite the incident.

items.originalTitle: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is ‘a great opportunity to go deceive people’
items.summary:
Tyler Shultz, the whistleblower who exposed Theranos' fraudulent blood testing technology, warns that the current AI boom presents a significant risk for deception as companies with unproven products raise capital at unprecedented valuations. He cautions that due diligence is difficult in AI investments, increasing the potential for misleading claims similar to those seen in the Theranos scandal.

Shultz highlights that Theranos raised large sums from individual investors without sharing scientific proof, a pattern he fears may repeat in AI startups. He also notes that Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos' founder, is preparing a new venture despite her conviction, raising concerns about the future of such high-profile tech fraud cases. His warnings come amid renewed public interest sparked by a documentary on Holmes and ongoing debates about investor responsibility in emerging technologies.

items.title: DoorDash CEO says outside AI agents have generated only hundreds of orders amid nearly 1 billion total in Q3 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Basically no one is using AI agents for their DoorDash orders
items.summary:
DoorDash CEO Tony Xu reported that third-party AI agents have accounted for only several hundred orders since their introduction, a negligible fraction of the nearly 1 billion orders processed in the third quarter of 2026. Xu described this as a very low use case, noting that simple tasks like food ordering tend to be done directly through DoorDash rather than via AI agents.

DoorDash recently launched its Model Context Protocol connector to facilitate AI agent ordering, but it remains in early beta with limited partners, mainly for corporate lunch orders. The company’s own AI tools, such as the Ask DoorDash feature, have shown more promising results by speeding up order creation and increasing basket value, though detailed usage statistics have not been disclosed. Xu expressed cautious optimism about AI agents’ potential for more complex purchases but remains realistic about their current adoption for food delivery.

items.title: Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite sends first AI-generated response from space using onboard TPU [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: We’ve received our first response from the Project Suncatcher prototype satellite.
items.summary:
Google launched its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite on October 1, 2026, aiming to explore AI compute capabilities in orbit. This week, the satellite successfully generated its first AI response—a haiku about space—using a data center-class TPU during a ground-station pass over Svalbard, Norway.

Following this milestone, the team tested additional AI-generated space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts to assess the satellite's technical status. Upcoming tests will evaluate TPU performance under thermal stress and radiation exposure, paving the way for a planned deployment of twin interconnected satellites in 2027 as part of this long-term research initiative.

items.originalTitle: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
items.summary:
DoorDash reported during its third-quarter earnings call that it has received only several hundred orders from third-party AI agents like Muse, Instinct, and Fo, compared to its average of 3 million daily deliveries. CEO Tony Xu noted that most users still place orders through the DoorDash app, but the company is interested in exploring agent-based ordering and collaborating with third-party agent developers.

DoorDash has launched its own AI ordering tools, including a text-to-order agent, a command-line interface agent, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash. The company also released a multi-channel platform to enable ordering through other chatbots for corporate clients. The broader market for AI agent ordering remains dynamic, with some retailers like Walmart welcoming agents while others like Amazon restrict their access.

items.originalTitle: Pope Leo calls for the disarmament of AI: ‘Machines are tools, not persons’
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV called for the disarmament of AI systems and urged United Nations member states to take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons during their upcoming meeting in Geneva. He emphasized that machines are tools, not persons, and stressed the importance of human responsibility in guiding, changing, or rejecting AI applications.

In his address, Pope Leo reiterated concerns from his earlier papal document about safeguarding human dignity amid AI advances, warning against granting AI systems rights or legal personhood. He called for international institutions to establish shared standards, independent oversight, and accountability mechanisms to manage AI development and use responsibly, ensuring decisions affecting human life and freedom remain under informed human control.

items.title: Fujifilm plans to increase magnetic tape production capacity fivefold by 2028 to meet rising data archiving demand driven by generative AI [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
items.summary:
Fujifilm announced a $63 million investment to expand its Kanagawa Factory's production of LTO Ultrium10 magnetic tape, aiming to quintuple output by fiscal year 2028. The company attributes the surge in tape demand to exponential data growth from generative AI and highlights tape's role in cost-effective, offline data storage and ransomware protection.

Magnetic tape remains widely used in enterprise and cloud data centers for backup due to its low cost and air-gap security benefits. Fujifilm's tape technology has evolved since the 1950s, with recent advances combining barium ferrite and strontium ferrite particles to increase storage capacity. The expansion reflects growing reliance on tape as a secure archival medium amid increasing cyber threats.

items.title: Runware plans to mass-produce modular AI data centers on an assembly line in Romania, targeting 30 megawatts daily capacity by 2028 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out
items.summary:
Runware is building a factory to assemble modular AI data centers, called Sonic Inference Pods, aiming to scale production to 30 megawatts per day by 2028, which would rival the entire US data center power additions this year. The company plans to reduce pod build time from three weeks to one day and bring pods online within 48 hours of installation, offering customization and rental options for customers.

Runware operates two factories in Romania, with a second facility expected to start production early next year. The company has raised over $60 million and plans a Series B funding round. It sources some components internationally but designs its own cooling and hardware systems. Runware claims to have received $1 billion in committed interest for its pods and is working with power providers on site pipelines totaling up to 1.2 gigawatts.

items.originalTitle: Behind DeepSeek’s $16 Billion Funding: Chinese Tech Titans and State Players
items.summary:
Chinese AI star DeepSeek’s nearly $16 billion funding round this month involved not only a deluge of capital but a who’s who of Chinese tech investors—and some of the country’s most powerful state-backed institutions, according to details of the round obtained by The Information.

It was only the second fundraising round for DeepSeek. The three-year-old company was the only major AI model developer to eschew external capital until its first fundraising in April. The new round included previous backers—Tencent and battery maker CATL continue to be DeepSeek’s top two investors—but also other tech companies including notably memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies and its chairman Zhu Yiming, according to the details provided by two people with direct knowledge of the matter.

items.title: DoorDash and Thrive Go Shopping [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DoorDash and Thrive Go Shopping
items.summary:
Get your deals in while ya still can, folks. And clearly, there are relative bargains to be had. 

DoorDash CEO Tony Xu gets what I’m talking about. On Thursday, Xu finally picked up Instacart, with Xu’s company saying it would pay about $17 billion for the grocery-delivery business. Over on X, Instacart founder Apoorva Mehta sent up a resounding huzzah, saying he and Xu had long discussed such a transaction. That wasn’t news to readers of The Information: We reported on talks between DoorDash and Instacart back in 2021.

At one point in 2021, DoorDash was considering buying Instacart for more than $40 billion. By waiting, Xu obviously saved himself a bunch of money and avoided the ridiculous markups that were attached to pandemic-era darlings like Instacart. Sure, its prospects seemed rosier back then, when we were regarding physical grocery stores as potentially lethal germ pools, but Xu doesn’t seem to be getting a total lemon. In the third quarter, Instacart sales grew 17%, and it generated a decent amount of cash in that time—more than $300 million, a 13% increase. 

The sale to Xu does solve Instacart’s leadership problem: It had looked rather rudderless since Fidji Simo left the CEO role for OpenAI in 2025. Still, Xu will need to figure out how to handle the fierce competition for online grocery sales, a battle that includes Walmart and Amazon (more on the latter company below). 

One thing that held Xu up in 2021 was concern about the Biden administration. Back then, Xu figured DoorDash wouldn’t get an Instacart acquisition past Biden regulators, who, of course, were trying their hardest to squelch corporate mergers and acquisitions. Those days of dealmaking famine have given way to a time of great feasting: The Trump White House has been, uh, lenient with regulatory approval. It could all shift once again after the midterms. With Democrats seemingly set to retake Congress next week, and President Donald Trump enjoying the same popularity as a DoorDasher who shows up with a carton of broken eggs, the idea of a liberal in the White House after 2028 seems a lot more plausible than it did even a few months ago. 

The prospect of a Democrat in the White House will spur plenty more M&A to happen sooner rather than later. I get it. Judging by the words of liberal standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, the left’s attitude toward mergers does not seem to have changed much since President Joe Biden creaked out of office. On Thursday, Mamdani criticized the DoorDash-Instacart deal, saying in a post on X that such moves often bring higher prices for consumers and “harsher exploitation” for workers. 

In addition to politics, M&A sure seems likely to keep humming for the simple reason that there are plenty of other Instacarts out there—businesses that haven’t fared well since their pandemic glory days. Zoom, Duolingo, Coursera: I could go on. I would’ve put Bumble right there, too, had it not already limped into the welcoming arms of investor Ravi Gupta several weeks ago. (Gupta bought Bumble for about $6 a share; Bumble once traded hands at more than $75.) Other M&A action seems like it’ll be driven by the chance to spruce up an aging business with AI, which I imagine is the motivating force behind the other deal announced on Thursday: Josh Kushner’s $7.6 billion purchase of ADT, maker of home security systems, through the newly formed Thrive Holdings, an offshoot of his Thrive Capital. 

Another reason that I’m going on and on about M&A today is because I listened to what Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett, the bank’s global co-head of investment banking, had to say about the topic at our WTF conference earlier this week. By the sounds of things, her direct messages are cluttered with missives from deal-hungry CEOs.

“They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape. CEOs are leaning in right now—they wanna make big strategic bets,” she said. “We’re optimistic.” Still, as she pointed out, “things change quickly.”—Abram Brown

Amazon’s Agita

If there’s a lesson in the earnings reports from Amazon and Google over the past couple of days, it’s that investors are more in the mood to focus on the companies’ blemishes rather than the strong performance of their cloud units. 

On Thursday, Amazon said revenues from its Amazon Web Services unit had surged 39% to $45.98 billion, its strongest growth rate in nearly five years. That was an impressive feat given that second-quarter AWS revenues grew at a record 37%. And if that wasn’t enough, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy forecast AWS growth rates of over 40% in 2027 and 2028. 

On a call with analysts, Jassy went even further and predicted that AWS could be one of two businesses for Amazon with $1 trillion a year revenue within the next five to 10 years (the other is its stores business—Amazon-speak for its e-commerce business and everything else, excluding AWS).

But, it turns out, that was not enough for investors, many of whom are increasingly on edge about whether tech giants will see a sustainable payoff from the colossal amounts of money they’re spending on AI. Amazon shares dropped more than 6% in after-hours trading. 

The company’s total net sales were $201.9 billion, up 12%, while its net income was $20.7 billion, down slightly from a year earlier, when it had a pre-tax gain of $9.5 billion from its investment in Anthropic. Even though Amazon’s numbers were within its own forecasts, Wall Street analysts were expecting slightly better results. The company left its estimate for its 2026 capital expenditures—most of which is going to its spending on data centers—unchanged at $220 billion.

Google had a similar experience today. Investors punished its stock, sending it down 12%. It appears they were more keen to focus on the bad in its Wednesday earnings report (sluggish revenue growth in its core search advertising business) rather than the good (a doubling of Google Cloud revenues). The AI glass seems to be half full for many investors right now.—Nick Wingfield

Correction: AWS’ growth rate in the third quarter of 2026 was the unit’s fastest in nearly five years. An earlier version of this newsletter misstated that figure.

In Other News

  • U.S. intelligence agencies found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese spy.
  • Coinbase’s latest earnings report showed the company had returned to profitability in the third quarter while sales had declined, underscoring how closely tied it remains to cryptocurrencies—despite a push to boost growth through new areas like prediction markets.
  • Intel shares plunged nearly 20% in after-hours trading after the firm said a slump in its business for PC processors would continue.
  • A suspected hack of Binance, a major crypto exchange, could involve billions of dollars.

items.summary:
Nvidia is in talks to provide Nscale, a young AI cloud provider, with billions of dollars in credit guarantees for debt to develop a 460-megawatt data center that Anthropic plans to use, according to people with knowledge of the deal discussions.

The deal is not yet signed, and terms could change. But it is another example of how Nvidia has continued to signal its financial support of so-called neoclouds like Nscale, CoreWeave and Firmus, which have faced pressure from investors because of the debt those companies have raised and will still need to raise to develop specialized data centers for AI.

items.title: Why Private Equity’s Fundraising Divide Is Pushing Newcomers Toward AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Private Equity’s Fundraising Divide Is Pushing Newcomers Toward AI
items.summary:
Private equity fundraising has become a story of haves and have-nots, as a prolonged slowdown in firms selling portfolio companies leaves investors with less cash to put into new funds. Giants like Blackstone are still raking in capital while some smaller firms struggle to attract investors, forcing newcomers to find creative ways to stand out. 

Some firms are betting that they can differentiate themselves by pushing AI to transform companies and boost returns. While larger private equity firms are also using AI across portfolio companies, such newcomers are making it central to their investment strategies. 

That includes Aldaron, which has dubbed itself a “transformation equity firm.” The 12-person firm uses an in-house team of engineers to deploy AI at the companies it acquires, though it emphasizes that its goal is to use the technology to grow businesses without cutting jobs. 

In a challenging private equity fundraising environment, “the core message that resonated with people is this transformation equity story,” said Aldaron co-founder Evan Mendez, who previously worked on technology investments at the Carlyle Group. He said the firm has a “hybrid group of investors and engineers that source a company, build the thesis together, cocreate a vision with the management team, underwrite the deal, put their own capital into the deal, and then embed into that company to go execute the road map.”

Aldaron completed its first acquisition in March, buying a majority stake in Oak Point Partners, an investment firm that buys remnant assets like IP and recovery claims. Aldaron funded that deal with money from early investors, some of which also made direct investments in Oak Point. Aldaron continued raising money afterward, closing its first fund in October with $884 million from outside investors and more than $950 million in total including the coinvestments, Mendez said.

The broader fundraising squeeze comes amid a yearslong slump in sales and initial public offerings of private equity–backed companies, leaving many firms with holdings they picked up in the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. Private equity firms are sitting on nearly 4,600 U.S. companies they’ve owned for at least five years, according to an August PitchBook report, longer than the industry’s typical three- to five-year holding period. That means less cash is returning to the pension funds, endowments and other investors, known as limited partners, leaving them with less money to commit to new funds. 

The biggest private equity firms often have an edge in competing for fresh capital thanks to their long track records, along with their sizable sales teams that allow them to reach various pools of capital including wealthy individual investors. Smaller fund managers, particularly those that are trying to raise their second or third funds after struggling to return money to investors, could be squeezed out entirely. 

“We expect many managers to exit the market, and we are already seeing this as fundraising becomes more challenging,” said Mitchell Mansfield, a managing director at Kroll and global head of fund solutions, which advises fund managers on restructuring and winding down funds. 

To be sure, leaning into AI is just one way smaller private equity firms are finding ways to distinguish themselves. Some are narrowing their focus to a particular sector rather than competing with funds that invest across industries. They can also offer investors more attractive terms, such as opportunities to coinvest in deals, often with lower fees. Fund managers can also put more of their own money into investments. 

Broadwing Capital Management, for instance, started buying companies before completing its first institutional fundraising, betting that an existing portfolio would help win over investors. “It’s a lot easier to talk about an investment with folks than about the theory of a new firm,” said co-founder and managing partner Eliot Kerlin, who launched Broadwing after 15 years at middle-market private equity firm Insight Equity. 

Broadwing, which focuses on manufacturing, industrial services and distribution businesses, launched in 2022 and made its first three acquisitions using money from outside investors and some of the founders’ own capital before hiring a placement agent to raise a larger fund. The firm structured its early investments so they could become part of a growing fund as Broadwing raised more money. The strategy paid off—Broadwing closed its $440 million inaugural fund this August, surpassing its fundraising goal by $90 million. By then it already owned six companies. 

Goldman Sachs Says CEOs Are ‘Leaning In’ on Strategic M&A

Strategic megadeals are dominating the tech mergers and acquisitions landscape right now, Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. That will likely continue, Posnett said, and the bank has a robust pipeline of deal talks across the board.

“They’re talking about really big deals, industry consolidation. They’re talking about M&A to bridge strategic gaps. They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape,” she said. 

“CEOs are leaning in right now and they want to make big strategic bets,” she said, noting that there’s “a ton of” strategic activity in tech specifically. Posnett’s comments came ahead of DoorDash’s Thursday announcement of a $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. (The Information was first to report last week that Instacart was in sale talks.)

items.title: ‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents
items.summary:
As Anthropic correctly pointed out in its initial public offering filing, business use of AI is in its infancy. Many other corporate executives say it will take some time for white-collar workers, especially those who aren’t software engineers, to use the latest tools effectively.

For example, White & Case, a large global law firm with more than 2,000 lawyers, is “having to hold back” its rollout of one of the newest legal assistants made by AI startup Legora because lawyers are hesitant about using so-called AI agents, said Isabel Parker, the law firm’s chief innovation officer. 

A gradual rollout will ensure lawyers feel confident in using the new agent, which can handle more complex legal work than the AI agent from Legora that lawyers currently use for tasks such as analyzing and summarizing documents and generating ideas, she said. Unlike simpler chatbots, AI agents can take multiple actions on behalf of the user.

Lawyers “are not the kind of people that easily lend themselves to using AI,” she told The Information’s Laura Mandaro during the WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women leaders in tech and finance. They’re “skeptical, they‘re time-poor, they’re risk averse, and they have a very strong conviction that their expertise is very artisanal...This technology comes along and it's a threat to everything they worked for.” 

Legora, a fast-growing app privately valued at roughly $9 billion, aims to automate legal work such as reviewing contracts and drafting documents—the kind of paperwork that needs to be error-free. In an email, Parker said White & Case is investing “significant amounts” in AI tools and that 90% of the firm’s staff uses Legora’s products to some extent. In some cases, using the products can save them as much as 80% of the time it took to manually perform tasks, she said.

Legora’s vice president of engagement, Jillian Burnett, said at the same event that the rapid pace of AI development means that lawyers must constantly learn new tools, which can wear them out.

“We’re working with a very skeptical [lawyer] client base overall, a very busy client base. And when they‘re already having to sit through trainings, different tools...lawyers aren’t necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new,” Burnett told Mandaro at the event.

She said Legora “didn't appreciate that fatigue enough” as a challenge to getting customers to use its tools. Legora has worked to address this by sending its staff to work with lawyers to show how the products can be “hyper-relevant” to their work.

Despite that resistance, Legora seems to be doing all right, and recently said it crossed $200 million in annualized recurring revenue. That implies it generates more than $16 million per month in revenue.

What is forcing change on White & Case lawyers is their clients. Parker said clients routinely ask the firm how it’s using new technologies to speed up work and how it can pass that “value” or new efficiencies to the clients. Now that both White & Case and the in-house legal teams of its clients often use the same AI apps and tools, “there’s nowhere to hide,” she said.

“One thing that cuts through any change fatigue in a lawyer is the client saying, ‘I want this done. Show me how you've been using this [AI tool],’” she said. 

In some cases, though, firms may intentionally slow AI use among junior employees to make sure they learn basic skills. For example, Parker said her firm is considering “sacrificing some efficiency” from AI so its junior lawyers can learn to do their work manually before adopting agents that can automate more difficult tasks such as Legora’s Agent Pro. 

“Most planes are flown by autopilot now...but you need to make sure that whoever's...in the cockpit does know how to fly a plane,” she said.
